nameStory: This fungus earned its "American Beefsteak" name because it looks remarkably like a raw piece of red meat when fresh, with a juicy, blood-like appearance that can actually drip reddish liquid when cut. It's the North American cousin of the European Beefsteak Polypore, discovered and named separately as our continent's own "meaty" mushroom. The scientific name Fistulina refers to the tiny tube-like pores on its underside, like miniature pipes.
description: The American Beefsteak Polypore is a striking bracket fungus that looks uncannily like a thick slab of raw beef attached to tree trunks. This meaty-looking mushroom can grow quite large, sometimes reaching 8-12 inches across and several inches thick. When fresh, it has a reddish-brown, tongue-like appearance with a soft, spongy texture that's unlike most other shelf fungi. Unlike typical polypores with their hard, woody texture, this one feels surprisingly soft and yielding to the touch.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Reddish-brown to deep red, tongue or liver-shaped bracket that's soft and spongy when fresh, often with a slightly sticky or moist surface that may have concentric zones

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Cream to pale yellow underneath with tiny individual tubes that can be separated easily with a fingernail, unlike most polypores where pores are fused together

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Usually grows directly from tree trunk without a stem, but sometimes has a short, thick, reddish stalk-like attachment point

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Cuts easily with a knife and may "bleed" a reddish juice when fresh, bruising darker red-brown where handled

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, slightly sour or tangy odor, sometimes described as faintly acidic or lemony

habitat: Look for American Beefsteak Polypore growing on living or recently dead hardwood trees, especially oaks, chestnuts, and occasionally maples throughout New England's mixed forests. It typically appears on the lower trunk or exposed roots of mature trees, often in areas where the tree has some stress or damage. You'll find it from sea level up into the mountains, wherever suitable hardwood hosts are present.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting may begin in late spring during warm, wet periods, appearing as small reddish bumps on host trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when fresh, soft specimens are most common. Look for the characteristic meaty appearance and soft texture during humid summer months.
seasonality.fall: Still actively growing through early fall, though specimens may become tougher and darker. This is often the best time to find large, mature brackets.
seasonality.winter: Old specimens persist as dark, hard, woody brackets that have lost their meaty appearance and soft texture, becoming more like typical shelf fungi.

funFact: When you cut into a fresh American Beefsteak Polypore, it can actually "bleed" red juice that looks so much like blood that it has fooled more than one hiker into thinking they've discovered some kind of wounded tree creature!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other reddish bracket fungi like Red-belted Polypore, but the American Beefsteak's uniquely soft, meaty texture when fresh is unmistakable - if you can poke your finger into it easily, you've likely found the right mushroom. Remember: hard brackets are something else entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the appetizing "beefsteak" name, this mushroom is generally considered too sour and tough for most palates, though it has been used historically as a meat substitute when properly prepared. Don't let the name fool you into thinking it's a gourmet find like some other edible polypores.
compareHints: Unlike its European relative the Beefsteak Polypore (Fistulina hepatica), the American species tends to be somewhat smaller and often has a more pronounced reddish coloration when young. Both share the distinctive soft texture and separable pore tubes that distinguish them from all other polypores in our region. If you find a bracket fungus that feels like raw meat, you're looking at one of the Fistulina species.
